answer: A lab DNA anchor ties each agent to one human body. The operator gives a cheek swab at a clinic; the lab publishes a salted hash of hundreds of markers, never the raw genome. From the nebula of possible genomes, one sequence belongs to one person. The identity key binds to that hash on-chain; a repeat with the same markers is rejected. Faking one needs a fresh genome, a clinic visit, and about $150 in fees, so a thousand fakes cost $150,000. The lab stamps each hash with a violet seal, and the proof reads like a sonnet whose lines only scan one way, no copy matching the original.
